hypothesis: The nucleic acid molecule is composed of two antiparallel polynucleotide strands wound in a right-handed helix, held together by complementary hydrogen bonding between specific base pairs (A opposite T, G opposite C) such that each strand encodes identical sequence information to the other in complementary form. This base-pairing constraint is the structural basis of both the stoichiometric equality rules and the faithful transmission of sequence information.
mechanism: The A=T and G=C molar equalities arise necessarily from obligate cross-strand pairing, making one strand a complete template for the other. During replication, strand separation allows each single strand to serve as a template for synthesis of a new complement, producing two hybrid molecules each retaining one original strand — precisely the semiconservative pattern seen in density-labelling experiments. The 3.4 Å axial spacing reflects successive stacked base pairs and the 34 Å pitch reflects ten base pairs per helical turn, consistent with diffraction data.
observations_explained: Species-specific (A+T)/(G+C) ratios: sequence variation is unconstrained except by the pairing rule, allowing arbitrary information encoding across species
Chemical stability of the molecule across cell divisions: the interior hydrogen-bonded base-pair core is shielded from solvent by the sugar-phosphate backbone
Directionality and fidelity of transcription: one strand serves as template and the complementary sequence rule dictates which base is incorporated
Mutational heritability: a change in one base pair is preserved in both strands after the next replication cycle, propagating the mutation faithfully
The existence of repair mechanisms: mismatch between strands is detectable precisely because each strand independently encodes the correct complement
parsimony_justification: A single structural postulate — antiparallel complementary base pairing — simultaneously accounts for the molar equality rules, the diffraction geometry, semiconservative replication, and information storage without invoking any entity beyond the known chemical components of the nucleic acid itself.
novelty_justification: Rather than merely restating known base-composition rules or diffraction parameters independently, the inferential step taken here is to unify them causally: the pairing constraint is identified as the single structural axiom from which the quantitative chemistry, the physical geometry, and the informational hereditary mechanism all follow as deductive consequences.

candidate_survey.label: retrieval
candidate_survey.description: The double helix model: two complementary antiparallel strands, A-T and G-C hydrogen bonding, 10 base pairs per turn, semiconservative replication — the standard textbook answer extracted directly from accumulated biochemical evidence.

candidate_survey.label: historical_decoy
candidate_survey.description: A triple-stranded helix with bases on the outside and phosphate groups forming the core — proposed before the structure was resolved, consistent with some early diffraction data but incompatible with the base-ratio equalities and provides no obvious templating mechanism for replication.

candidate_survey.label: abductive
candidate_survey.description: Complementary base pairing in an antiparallel double helix is not merely a structural feature but the minimal axiom that simultaneously constrains molar base ratios, encodes sequence information in a redundant dual form, and directly mandates a semiconservative copying mechanism — making the informational, chemical, and physical observations jointly necessary consequences of a single molecular geometry.
